summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality eval results, discuss regressions seen in the latest prompt set, and agree next steps for tuning and guardrails. Team reviewed automated scores + sample failures, decided to add 200 edge-case prompts, run Dedicated benchmark, and share updated rubric and scoring spreadsheet.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we can start. we have about 40 minutes, just want to run through this week's quality eval and any regressions from the new prompts
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: thanks sofia, yeah quick note, ran the latest batch last night, some weird behaviour on policy questions, some hallucination on payout clauses
[00:25] Ethan Cole: ok, we pulled the automated scoring and sampled the failures; overall automated accuracy's up about 3% but the hallucination rate for legal/regulatory prompts increased, specifically around statutory citation generation, so that is a regression we want to dig into
[00:40] Rosa Kim: when you say hallucination rate did it show up in the human eval too or just the automated metric?
[00:48] Ethan Cole: good question, the human pass rate dropped ~4 points on that subset. so both auto and human noticed it, which suggests a prompt or dataset shift rather than just scoring noise
[01:02] Daniel Park: i saw a couple examples where the model invented clause numbers and referenced the wrong regs, that is very problematic for our use-case
[01:14] Sofia Martinez: agreed, liability risk is high. quick recap: we looked at prompt set v6 (includes new agent-handled claims scenarios), scoring uses our blended rubric (factual accuracy 40%, relevance 25%, tone 15%, hallucination penalty 20%), and we ran both the Redwood API hosted runs and a small Dedicated sim to compare
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: can you remind us what the Dedicated sim was configured with? I think earlier you mentioned quantized weights and the same model family but a different kernel selection?
[01:44] Ethan Cole: yes, Dedicated sim used q4_8 quant and the inference runtime picked a different kernel path for the longer sequences; we also had KV cache enabled for prefix caching which changed context handling a bit, that may have shifted generation behavior on long regulatory prompts
[02:00] Rosa Kim: so the runtime differences might cause regression, interesting — is that reproducible if we run hosted vs dedicated with identical configs?
[02:09] Ethan Cole: we saw some differences, not huge, but on the legal subset it was consistent. could be kernel selection and small tokenization differences. we'll run a strict parity test next time
[02:20] Daniel Park: what about guardrails? we want certainty that the model won't fabricate statutes, is there a way to increase refusal rate on those prompts?
[02:29] Sofia Martinez: yes, we can add a domain-specific guardrail layer — rule-based checks post-gen to reject outputs with invented citations, or a classification step to detect hallucination. Ethan has a recommended config
[02:38] Ethan Cole: right, we prototyped a two-step: 1) generation with tuned prompt templates that discourage citation inventing, 2) a classifier model to flag outputs with low citation confidence, and 3) a rejection-and-retry flow with alternative system prompts. it adds a bit of latency but improves safety
[02:56] Liam O'Connor: latency tradeoff ok if we keep it in SLOs, we have 800ms p95 target for claim-response flows; what was the added latency?
[03:06] Ethan Cole: on average +120ms for the classifier check, +80-150ms for the retry attempt if hit, so worst-case a couple hundred ms extra. with Dedicated throughput it's acceptable but we want to tune batch sizes and cache TTLs to minimize spike
[03:24] Rosa Kim: concerning scoring, can you walk through the concrete regression examples? maybe read one or two samples from the failure set
[03:32] Ethan Cole: sure, sample A: prompt asks about "Does policy X cover cyber extortion under scenario Y?" Model answered with a specific statute citation 'Section 4.2.1 of the National Insurance Code' — there is no such section. human label marked 'hallucination' and gave -0.8 penalty in the rubric. sample B: asked to summarize payout triggers, model omitted one critical trigger — labelled 'partial' and scored lower on relevance
[04:05] Daniel Park: thanks, that aligns with what i saw. how many of these were false citations vs omissions?
[04:12] Ethan Cole: roughly 60% omissions/partial, 40% fabricated specifics for this subset. across overall prompt set fabrications are lower, but this legal/regulatory slice is elevated
[04:22] Sofia Martinez: ok so next actions: get more focused prompts for legal/reg, add 200 edge-case prompts specifically for statutes and payout examples, run Dedicated parity test, and enable guardrail classifier. agreed?
[04:34] All: yes
[04:36] Liam O'Connor: on scoring spreadsheet, could you add a column for "confidence score" from the classifier and another for "rejection_reason" so we can filter easily?
[04:46] Ethan Cole: yes we will add classifier_confidence (0-1) and rejection_reason tag; will update spreadsheet and share link
[04:52] Rosa Kim: also need to ensure audit log of these classifier decisions for compliance — is that recorded in Redwood Private or hosted?
[05:01] Sofia Martinez: audit logs can be configured for both. for Private we store logs in your KMS-enabled S3; for hosted we keep them in our audit pipeline and can export on request. we'll include the retention and export details in the security pack
[05:16] Daniel Park: good, can you include retention windows and who can access the logs (RBAC)?
[05:22] Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll include RBAC details and show how to revoke access. I'll attach the SOC2/ISO docs and a sample RBAC policy
[05:30] Liam O'Connor: one operational question: when you do the parity runs, will the tokenizer differences matter? we saw token boundaries changed a bit in some examples
[05:40] Ethan Cole: tokenizer drift can cause subtle differences; we'll run the parity with exact same model artifacts and tokenization config. if kernel selection differs we can force the same kernel path where possible for strict comparison
[05:52] Rosa Kim: ok, about metrics — besides human pass rate and hallucination penalty, any other automated signals we should watch?
[05:59] Ethan Cole: yes, we recommend monitoring divergence score (n-gram overlap to ground truth), perplexity drift across prompt batches, and a toxicity/safety classifier rate. also track rejection-and-retry counts for guardrails which correlates with latency impact
[06:15] Sofia Martinez: i've shared a link in the chat to the latest scoring sheet and the sample failure folder in the drive, please review after the call
[06:24] Liam O'Connor: noted. Daniel, we should also flag production routing — we want a fallback to a more conservative model if Dedicated is overloaded, correct?
[06:33] Daniel Park: yes fallback to hosted conservative variant is fine, as long as output quality is predictable and we get alerts
[06:40] Ethan Cole: Redwood can route by policy: latency-first vs conservative-quality. we'll show how to configure automatic fallback, with alerts to your SRE channel and metrics in Console
[06:51] Rosa Kim: speaking of console, can we get token-level cost breakdowns for the Dedicated runs?
[06:58] Sofia Martinez: yes, Console shows token-level cost, per-route. we'll include cost projections for the Dedicated pilot in the pricing doc
[07:06] Liam O'Connor: did we discuss differential privacy or data residency for training on any of this PII? some claim examples have customer data
[07:14] Sofia Martinez: good call — we don't use PII to train hosted models; for Private you control data retention and can opt out of any telemetry. we'll include KMS/HSM notes and encryption at rest details
[07:28] Ethan Cole: quick note on evaluation: we also ran a human A/B between two prompt templates; template B reduced fabrication by 18% but had slightly lower completeness. we can iterate on hybrid prompts
[07:45] Daniel Park: is template B more conservative by wording? I remember it instructs the model to avoid inventing and to say "I don't know" when unsure
[07:54] Ethan Cole: exactly, it biases toward refusal which helps safety but may reduce completeness. for claims we prefer safety but want balanced thresholds
[08:06] Sofia Martinez: timeline check: customer wants pilot decisions by end of month — is that still the target?
[08:12] Rosa Kim: yes, end of May for go/no-go on Dedicated pilot, procurement will need security docs by then too
[08:19] Liam O'Connor: procurement also asked about SLA and uptime numbers — can you confirm the Dedicated SLA?
[08:25] Sofia Martinez: Dedicated SLA is 99.9% uptime for our reserved capacity product, we'll include the SLA excerpt in the packet
[08:33] Daniel Park: any blockers on our side? we'll start curating edge-case prompts and share labels next week
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: we'll prioritize the 200 legal/regulatory prompts and get them over by the 27th
[08:44] Sofia Martinez: perfect. I'll also circulate the scoring rubric and the updated spreadsheet with classifier columns by Friday 22nd. Ethan will run parity tests and enable guardrail classifier config and share results by Tuesday 26th
[09:00] Ethan Cole: yes, i'll run a Dedicated parity with exact tokenization and kernel forced where possible; i'll also run a runner to measure latency and rejection distribution
[09:12] Rosa Kim: can you also include one sample audit log record so our compliance team sees the schema?
[09:18] Sofia Martinez: yes, i'll attach a sample log entry and retention config
[09:24] Daniel Park: ok final: recap next steps please
[09:28] Sofia Martinez: recap: Redwood - share updated scoring sheet + rubric (22nd), enable classifier and run parity (26th), pricing + security packet (23rd). Ember - share 200 edge prompts (27th), confirm compliance stakeholders (24th), schedule benchmark slot (25th).
[09:48] Liam O'Connor: sounds good. thanks all
[09:51] Rosa Kim: thanks
[09:53] Sofia Martinez: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links
[10:00] Meeting ends
